newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil drops resistance to nuclear weapons treaty.
newsitem.headline: Brazil drops resistance to nuclear weapons treaty.

text.p: President Fernando Henrique Cardoso asked Congress on Friday to approve adherence to the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty (NPT), ending Brazil's 27 years of resistance to the arms pact.

"This is an important moment for Brazil's international relations," he told officials after signing documents related to the treaty. "The accords signed here are a legally perfect guarantee that Brazil will not develop a nuclear weapon."
Brazil is one of only five nations that have not signed the NPT, which came into effect in 1970. The country was then a military dictatorship with secret nuclear ambitions.

Successive governments have refused to sign the treaty, saying it favoured established nuclear powers, which were not bound to give up their weapons. But Cardoso's administration, seeking to bury Brazil's isolationist past, sees adherence as another step toward raising the country's profile.

"Much has changed since the Cold War," Cardoso said in his speech. "There is ever-greater convergence of the objective of nuclear disarmament and nonproliferation. ... It was time we decided to influence the process from within."
He said he welcomed cuts to U.S. and Russian nuclear arsenals but the reductions should be sped up and be followed by other nuclear nations.

Brazil's 1988 constitution prohibited the use of nuclear power for nonpeaceful purposes and the country is a signatory of the 1994 Tlatelolco Treaty, which prohibited nuclear weapons throughout Latin America.

Friday's announcement came a day before Cardoso travels to New York for next week's special environment summit at the United Nations. Brazil has been lobbying long and hard for a seat on the Security Council if it is expanded in the future.
